summary: This informational RFC was published on April 1 and is humorous. It claims to define the Null Packet, which earlier RFCs mentioned many times without defining it. It should not be taken as a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke about a packet that has nothing in it. It is an April Fools' joke, so do not take it seriously.

subtitle: An April 1st RFC humorously defining a packet that contains nothing.

tldr.problem: The Null Packet had been mentioned in many RFCs but never formally defined. This April 1st RFC corrects that omission by defining a zero-dimensional packet that is non-self-contradictory.
tldr.mechanism: The Null Packet cannot have a protocol ID, cannot be sent or acknowledged when not received, and exists because it is non-self-contradictorily definable.
tldr.outcome: The Null Packet is defined (or not defined, depending on your perspective). It remains a theoretical construct and a running joke in networking standards.

today: RFC 6592 is an Informational, April 1st RFC. It is a humor document and was never intended for implementation. The Null Packet remains a theoretical construct and a running joke in the networking community.

sections.title: The Elusive Null Packet
sections.content:
Many RFCs reference the Null Packet, but it was never formally defined. This April 1st RFC corrects that omission. The Null Packet is described as a zero-dimensional packet that is non-self-contradictorily definable, so it exists. Van Jacobson mentioned it in the context of TCP/IP header compression (RFC 1144), describing an explicit lack of response as "Nothing (a null packet) is returned."

The Null Packet cannot have a protocol ID, because the existence of any protocol construct would "null the null." It cannot be 0x0, 0x0000, or any numeric value—though the empty string "" is oddly permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs talked about "null packets" without saying what they are. This joke RFC finally "defines" it: it is a packet with absolutely nothing in it.

sections.title: Security and the Paradox
sections.content:
The RFC explores whimsical security properties. The Null Packet cannot have the Evil Bit (RFC 3514) set, so it is harmless. In MPLS environments, it can only use an Implicit NULL label, which never appears in the encapsulation. Firewalls have trouble with it: they may claim to both filter it out and let it through, creating a paradox. The RFC humorously asks: can a firewall block Null Packets coming in while allowing them out?

One unexpected benefit: attacks using Null Packets are rare, perhaps because they are hard to spoof in the data plane, and Null Packets present a "denial of denial of service" (DoDoS) by being unblockable.
sections.plainLanguage: Security people joke about the Null Packet being impossible to block, yet harmless.

sections.title: Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The Null Packet has peculiar performance properties. Sending more Null Packets does not increase the bit rate (it remains zero). Stopping transmission of Null Packets also does not change the bit rate (still zero). Traditional traffic metrics are unsuited to measure Null Packet performance, so the RFC cheekily argues for new performance metrics that "test positive for usefulness."

In a humorous aside, the RFC notes that the section on the formal definition of the Null Packet is intentionally left blank, referencing itself and RFC 7.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet with nothing in it has zero bandwidth. Even sending a trillion of them costs zero bandwidth.
